title: Advantages, Limitations, and Shared Responsibility
subtopics: Vendor dependency and cloud migration considerations
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of advantages, limitations, and shared responsibility and its relationship to Introduction to AWS and Cloud Computing.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to advantages, limitations, and shared responsibility.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn advantages, limitations, and shared responsibility in the context of Introduction to AWS and Cloud Computing. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: Advantages, Limitations, and Shared Responsibility matters because it is one part of cloud concepts and service selection. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: Module 1: Introduction to AWS and Cloud Computing
content_blocks.alt_text: Five-step overview for module 1, Introduction to AWS and Cloud Computing, followed by verification, least-privilege security, recovery, and cost-cleanup checks.
content_blocks.caption: Module 1 learning sequence: understand the concept, make a controlled design/configuration, verify behavior, and document security/reliability/cost trade-offs.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Advantages, Limitations, and Shared Responsibility belongs to Introduction to AWS and Cloud Computing. Start from the cloud model, then learn how to describe a workload and map its needs to AWS service categories.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Scalability and availability; Usage-based pricing and operational trade-offs; Vendor dependency and cloud migration considerations; AWS responsibility versus customer responsibility. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For advantages, limitations, and shared responsibility, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Scalability and availability
items.text: Define the failure scenario and recovery objective, then test detection, recovery, data consistency and rollback. Treat recovery evidence as a deliverable, not an assumption.

items.title: Usage-based pricing and operational trade-offs
items.text: Estimate the complete workload, including requests, storage, data transfer and dependent services. Compare the estimate with actual usage and alerts; an alert is not a hard spend cap.

items.title: Vendor dependency and cloud migration considerations
items.text: Write a verification step and a failure case. For hands-on work, start with read-only inspection and use an approved sandbox before changing cloud resources.

items.title: AWS responsibility versus customer responsibility
items.text: Record ownership, dependencies and teardown/recovery behavior so the design can be operated safely after the first successful test.

content_blocks.title: Workload sketch: Advantages, Limitations, and Shared Responsibility
content_blocks.expected_output: A small architecture decision record that can be reviewed before any resource is created.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This block is an inspectable example, not an AWS action performed by CodeLeaf. Review the example as text and adapt it only after checking current official service documentation. Do not apply/deploy changes in a real account without account-owner approval, least-privilege permissions and a reviewed cost/cleanup plan.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No AWS resource is created by this lesson example. If you independently run an approved lab, capture the starting state first, follow the lab-specific teardown instructions, check dependent resources and billing/resource inventories, and document anything retained.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview and does not execute AWS APIs, shell commands, SQL or cloud deployments. Treat output as illustrative; live values depend on credentials, permissions, Region, service state and schema.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “Advantages, Limitations, and Shared Responsibility”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for Advantages, Limitations, and Shared Responsibility with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: Advantages, Limitations, and Shared Responsibility is taught as part of Introduction to AWS and Cloud Computing.
Start from the cloud model, then learn how to describe a workload and map its needs to AWS service categories.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
